summary: Defines a profile for using X.509 Attribute Certificates in Internet protocols. Attribute certificates bind attributes such as roles or permissions to a holder, and may be used for authorization across a range of environments. It is on the standards track.

plainLanguage.summary: A public key certificate says who you are. An attribute certificate says what you are allowed to do, and it comes from a different authority that says so. This document fixes the shape of those certificates, so that any two programs that follow it can read each other's and check them the same way.

subtitle: A common shape for the certificates that say who may do what, and where.

tldr.problem: Authorization data such as group membership or clearance often has a different lifetime and a different authority than the identity-and-key binding in a public key certificate, so stuffing it into that certificate works poorly.
tldr.mechanism: The profile constrains the X.509 attribute certificate, a signed structure with a holder, an issuer, a validity period and attributes but no public key. It fixes which fields, extensions, attribute types, validation rules and revocation schemes implementations must support.
tldr.outcome: It is a Proposed Standard that obsoletes RFC 3281, correcting errata and clarifying details, and gives generic applications a common baseline for attribute certificates.

facts.label: Audit identity length
facts.value: More than 0 and no more than 20 octets

facts.label: Time format
facts.value: YYYYMMDDHHMMSSZ in UTC, no fractional seconds

today: RFC 5755 is a Proposed Standard published in January 2010. It obsoletes RFC 3281 and has not been obsoleted or updated since, so it remains the standard profile for using X.509 attribute certificates for authorization.

sections.title: Why an Attribute Certificate
sections.content:
X.509 public key certificates bind an identity and a public key. An attribute certificate is a structure similar to a public key certificate, with one main difference: it contains no public key. An attribute certificate may contain attributes that specify group membership, role, security clearance, or other authorization information associated with the holder. The syntax for it is defined in Recommendation X.509, which makes the term "X.509 certificate" ambiguous.

The document offers an analogy to make the distinction clear. A public key certificate is like a passport: it identifies the holder, tends to last a long time, and should not be trivial to obtain. An attribute certificate is more like an entry visa: it is typically issued by a different authority and does not last as long. As acquiring an entry visa typically requires presenting a passport, getting a visa can be a simpler process.

Authorization information may be placed in a public key certificate extension or in a separate attribute certificate. Putting it in the certificate is usually undesirable for two reasons. First, authorization information often does not have the same lifetime as the binding of the identity and the public key, and the general result of placing it in the extension is to shorten the useful lifetime of the certificate. Second, the certificate issuer is not usually the authority for the authorization information, so the issuer has to take extra steps to obtain it from the authoritative source.

For these reasons it is often better to separate authorization information from the public key certificate. The authorization information still has to be bound to an identity, and the attribute certificate provides that binding: it is a digitally signed identity and set of attributes. It may be used with various security services, including access control, data origin authentication and non-repudiation.

Public key certificates can give an identity to an access control decision function. In many contexts, however, the identity is not the criterion used for the decision; the role or group membership of the accessor is, and such schemes are called role-based access control. When the decision is based on an attribute certificate, the verifier may need to ensure that the certificate holder is the entity that requested access. One way to achieve that linkage is to include a reference to a public key certificate inside the attribute certificate and use the private key of that certificate to authenticate within the access request.

The profile also sets out the requirements it has to meet: support for short-lived as well as long-lived certificates, so that a certificate can be useful without any revocation mechanism; the ability for issuers to define their own attribute types within closed domains; a set of standard attribute types such as access identity, group, role and clearance; standard attribute types defined so that a verifier can tell uses of the same name in different domains apart; the ability to target a certificate at one or a small number of servers, so that a trustworthy non-target server rejects it; and the ability for a certificate to be either pushed by the client to the server or pulled by the server from a repository or an online issuer.

Finally, the document deals with delegation. The X.509 standard defines authorization as the conveyance of privilege from one entity that holds it to another, and an ordered sequence of attribute certificates could be used to verify the authenticity of a privilege asserter's privilege. Since the administration and processing of such chains is complex and the use of attribute certificates on the Internet today is quite limited, it is RECOMMENDED that implementations of this specification not use such chains. This specification deals with the simple case, where one authority issues all the certificates for a particular set of attributes, but that does not preclude several authorities each managing a different set of attributes: group membership might be in one certificate issued by one authority and security clearance in another issued by another. Conformant implementations are therefore only REQUIRED to process a single certificate at a time, although validating one MAY require validating a chain of public key certificates.
sections.plainLanguage: A passport says who you are and lasts for years. A visa says what you may do here and lasts for months, and a different office issues it. Attribute certificates work the second way: they carry permissions and roles instead of a public key, and they are issued by whoever is authoritative about those permissions.

sections.title: How the Certificate Reaches the Server
sections.content:
Attribute certificates provide a mechanism to securely provide authorization information to, for example, access control decision functions, but there are a number of possible communication paths for them.

In some environments it is suitable for a client to "push" a certificate to a server. That means no new connections between the client and the server are required, no search burden is imposed on servers, which improves performance, and the verifier is only presented with what it needs to know. The push model is especially suitable in inter-domain cases where the client's rights should be assigned within the client's home domain.

In other cases it is more suitable for a client to authenticate to the server and for the server to request or "pull" the client's certificate from an issuer or a repository. A major benefit of the pull model is that it can be implemented without changes to the client or to the client-server protocol. The pull model is especially suitable in inter-domain cases where the client's rights should be assigned within the server's domain rather than within the client's domain.

There are a number of possible exchanges involving three entities: the client, the server and the certificate issuer. A directory service or other repository for certificate retrieval MAY also be supported. The profile does not specify a protocol for these exchanges, only the shape of the certificate that travels through them.
sections.plainLanguage: The certificate can travel in either direction. The client can send it along with the request, which is fast and cheap, or the server can fetch it from whoever issued it, which needs no change to the client. The document describes the possible exchanges but does not define a protocol for them.

sections.title: The Structure of an Attribute Certificate
sections.content:
An attribute certificate is a sequence of three parts: an information structure, a signature algorithm identifier and a signature value. The information structure holds the version, the holder, the issuer, the signature algorithm, the serial number, the validity period, the attributes, an optional issuer unique identifier and optional extensions. The version is v2.

The Holder field is a sequence allowing three optional syntaxes: baseCertificateID, which is the issuer and serial number of the holder's public key certificate; entityName, which is the name of the claimant or role; and objectDigestInfo, which is used to authenticate the holder directly, for example an executable. The issuer field is a choice between the v1 form, which MUST NOT be used in this profile, and the v2 form, which carries the issuer's name and is the one to use. The validity period is a pair of times, notBeforeTime and notAfterTime, in the GeneralizedTime type.

Each attribute carries a type, which is an object identifier, and a set of values, with at least one value required. Implementers should note that the DER encoding of the set of values requires ordering the encodings of the values. That issue arises with distinguished names too and has to be handled by public key certificate implementations, but it is much more significant here, since including multiple values is much more common in attribute certificates.
sections.plainLanguage: The certificate has the same shape as a public key certificate: a body of information, the algorithm used to sign it and the signature. The body names the holder and the issuer, gives a serial number and a validity period, and lists the attributes. What it does not have is a public key.

sections.title: The Profile of the Standard Fields
sections.content:
The profile constrains the use of GeneralName, which offers great flexibility. Conforming implementations MUST be able to support the dNSName, directoryName, uniformResourceIdentifier and iPAddress options, and SHOULD also support the SRVName. They MUST NOT use the x400Address, ediPartyName or registeredID options, and MAY use the otherName option to convey name forms defined in Internet Standards, such as Kerberos principal names.

The version field MUST have the value v2. The Holder field SHOULD use the baseCertificateID where the certificate is passed in an authenticated session based on an X.509 public key certificate; the holder's certificate serial number and issuer must then be identical to the AC holder field. The specification RECOMMENDS that only one of the three holder options be used in any given certificate, since where more than one is used there is a potential for confusion about which is normative.

The issuer MUST use the v2 form with exactly one GeneralName in the issuerName, containing a non-empty distinguished name, so all issuers have non-empty distinguished names, and the baseCertificateID and objectDigestInfo fields MUST be omitted. One reason is that the issuer then does not have to know which public key certificate the verifier will use for it; referencing the issuer's own certificate would force the verifier to trust the certificate the issuer chose for itself at creation time.

The signature algorithm MUST be one of those defined in the public key certificate algorithms document. The issuer and serial number pair MUST form a unique combination even for short-lived certificates, and issuers MUST force the serial number to be a positive integer. AC users MUST be able to handle serial numbers longer than 4 octets, and conforming certificates MUST NOT contain serial numbers longer than 20 octets. The numbers need not be monotonically increasing with time, but each issuer MUST ensure that each certificate it issues has a unique serial number.

The validity period says for how long the issuer certifies the binding between the holder and the attributes. Times MUST be expressed in Coordinated Universal Time and MUST include seconds, and MUST NOT include fractional seconds. AC users MUST be able to handle a certificate whose validity period lies partly or wholly in the past or in the future, which some applications use for backup.

The attributes field gives information about the holder and often a set of privileges. Each attribute type may occur only once in a given certificate, but each occurrence may carry several values, and AC users MUST be able to handle multiple values for all attribute types. A certificate MUST contain at least one attribute. The issuer unique identifier MUST NOT be used unless it is also used in the issuer's own public key certificate, in which case it MUST be used. An unrecognized critical extension must cause the certificate to be rejected, while an unrecognized non-critical extension may be ignored.
sections.plainLanguage: The profile pins down the loose ends: which kinds of name are allowed, that the issuer is named rather than referenced by certificate, that serial numbers are unique and positive, that times are written in one fixed format, and that a certificate must carry at least one attribute.

sections.title: The Standard Attribute Types
sections.content:
Some of the standard attribute types use the IetfAttrSyntax type, which allows a separation between the certificate issuer and the attribute policy authority. That is useful where one organisation allocates attribute values but several issuers are deployed. The syntax also restricts the values to an octet string, an object identifier or a UTF8 string, which reduces the complexity of matching, and every value of a multi-valued attribute must use the same choice of syntax, so an issuer must not use one value with an object identifier and a second value with a string.

The service authentication information attribute identifies the holder to the server or service by a name and may include service-specific authentication information, typically a username and password for a legacy application. It is presented by the verifier to be interpreted and authenticated by a separate application within the target system, and it will typically be encrypted when it holds a password.

The access identity attribute identifies the holder to the server or service for authorization decisions, and its authInfo field MUST NOT be present. The charging identity attribute identifies the holder for charging purposes and in general differs from the holder's other identities, for example because the holder's company is charged for the service.

The group attribute carries information about the group memberships of the holder. The role attribute, specified in X.509, carries information about role allocations, with an optional roleAuthority field naming the authority that issued the role specification and a roleName field that MUST be present and MUST use the uniformResourceIdentifier choice. That field lets the same role name from two different authorities be told apart, for example by putting "urn:administrator" in the roleName and the name of the authority in the roleAuthority.

The clearance attribute carries the security clearance information of the holder. Its policyId field identifies the security policy the clearance relates to, which gives the meaning of the class list and the security categories. The basic classification hierarchy in ascending order is unmarked, unclassified, restricted, confidential, secret and top-secret, and the bit string positions 0 through 5 are reserved for it. Additional classification values may be defined locally or by bilateral agreement. The security categories field adds further authorization information, with the syntaxes allowed there set by the policy.
sections.plainLanguage: Six attribute types are defined: which name the holder has for a service, which name to use for access decisions, which name to bill, which groups the holder is in, which role the holder has, and what security clearance the holder has. The profile also defines a simple way of writing them, so that checking them stays easy.

sections.title: Extensions for Targeting and Revocation
sections.content:
The audit identity extension exists for cases where an audit trail must not contain records that directly identify individuals, for example under data protection or privacy legislation. The audit identity value, together with the issuer and serial number, is then used for audit and logging, so that an administrator can track the behaviour of a holder without being able to identify the holder. The issuer must be able to determine the actual identity of the holder from the audit identity, so that the holder can be identified if misbehaviour is detected. The extension MUST be critical when used, and its value must be longer than zero octets and no longer than 20 octets.

The target information extension names the servers or services the certificate may be used at. An honest verifier that is not among the named targets must reject the certificate, and if the extension is absent the certificate is not targeted and may be accepted by any server. The targets check passes if the current server is one of the target names, or is a member of one of the target groups; how that membership is determined is not defined here, for example a group might name a DNS domain and the verifier knows its own domain.

The authority key identifier extension may help the verifier check the signature and should be included. The authority information access extension points at revocation information, for example an OCSP responder reached over HTTP. The CRL distribution points extension points at a revocation list, with exactly one distribution point holding a single name that is either a distinguished name or a URI using HTTP or LDAP. The no revocation available extension says that no revocation information will be published for this certificate; it must be non-critical.

Four optional features may be implemented, and if they are offered they must be offered as described. Attributes may be encrypted using the Cryptographic Message Syntax EnvelopedData structure, with the ciphertext carried in an encAttrs attribute; the encrypted content also carries the issuer and serial number, so that a verifier can detect ciphertext stolen from another certificate. Proxying, where a server acts as a client on behalf of a user, is handled by a proxy information extension that lists targets, and the verifier must check that the entity it received the certificate from was allowed to send it. The objectDigestInfo holder choice links a certificate to an object by a hash, and this profile only specifies how to hash a public key or a public key certificate. The AA controls extension, used in the issuer's own public key certificate, answers the question of whether that issuer is trusted to issue certificates with a given attribute: it may restrict the permitted and excluded attribute types and the distance to the issuer.
sections.plainLanguage: Extensions add the extra behaviour that a plain certificate cannot carry: naming the servers the certificate may be used at, saying where revocation information lives, giving an audit trail a value that hides the holder's name, encrypting the attributes, and limiting what the issuer may put in a certificate at all.

sections.title: Validation and Revocation
sections.content:
To be valid, an attribute certificate must satisfy all of the following. Where the holder uses a public key certificate to authenticate to the verifier, the holder's certificate must be found and its entire certification path verified. The certificate's signature must be cryptographically correct and the issuer's entire certification path must be verified. The issuer's own certificate must conform to the profile, which requires that the issuer is not also a certificate authority. The issuer must be directly trusted as an issuer of attribute certificates, by configuration or otherwise. The time of evaluation must fall within the validity period, with the check passing if it equals either boundary, and in some applications the evaluation time may not be the current time. The targeting check must pass. And a certificate with an unsupported critical extension must be rejected. Supporting an extension means the verifier can parse it and will reject the certificate when the extension value says so.

Additional checks are optional: the verifier may reject a certificate on the basis of its own configuration, for example by requiring certain attributes to be present, and it may filter the attributes it returns to applications.

In many environments the validity period of a certificate is less than the time required to issue and distribute revocation information, so short-lived certificates typically need no revocation support, while long-lived certificates and environments where certificates enable high value transactions may need it. Two schemes are defined. Under the "never revoke" scheme, the noRevAvail extension is present and says that no revocation status will be made available; where it is absent, the issuer is implicitly stating that revocation checks are supported and some method MUST be provided. Under the "pointer in AC" scheme, the certificate points at sources of revocation status information through an authority information access or a CRL distribution points extension.

For AC users the "never revoke" scheme MUST be supported and the "pointer in AC" scheme SHOULD be supported. If only the "never revoke" scheme is supported, then all certificates that do not contain the noRevAvail extension MUST be rejected. For issuers the "never revoke" scheme MUST be supported, and the "pointer in AC" scheme MUST also be supported if any certificate can be issued without the noRevAvail extension. A certificate MUST NOT contain both a noRevAvail extension and a pointer in AC.
sections.plainLanguage: A verifier has a checklist of seven conditions before it will rely on a certificate, and it may add its own. For revocation there are two schemes: either the certificate says no revocation information will ever be published, or it points at where to find it.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The protection of private keys is a critical factor in maintaining security. Failure of issuers to protect their private keys permits an attacker to masquerade as them, potentially generating false certificates or revocation status, which undermines confidence in the system. If the compromise is detected, all certificates issued by that issuer MUST be revoked, and rebuilding after such a compromise is problematic. Issuers are advised to combine strong technical measures such as tamper-resistant cryptographic modules with management procedures such as separation of duties. Loss of a signing key is also problematic, since the issuer could then neither produce revocation status nor renew certificates, so secure backup is advised.

The availability and freshness of revocation status affects how much assurance to place in a long-lived certificate. Events during its lifetime can negate the binding between holder and attributes, and if revocation status is untimely or unavailable the assurance is clearly reduced. The binding between a holder and its attributes cannot be stronger than the cryptographic module and algorithms used to sign, so short keys or weak hash algorithms limit the utility of a certificate.

Inconsistent application of name comparison rules may lead to acceptance of invalid targeted or proxied certificates, or rejection of valid ones. This specification relaxes the X.500 rules and requires support for binary comparison at a minimum. Issuers MUST encode the distinguished name in the holder's entityName field identically to the distinguished name in the holder's certificate, or implementations may fail to recognize that the two belong to the same entity.

If a certificate is tied to the holder's certificate through the baseCertificateID and the public key infrastructure includes a rogue authority with the same issuer name and serial number, that authority could issue a certificate to a malicious party that could then be used with the attribute certificate. This should be avoided by managing the infrastructure so that two authorities cannot share a name, or by tying certificates with the publicKeyCert type in the objectDigestInfo field instead. Failing that, verifiers have to establish by other means that such collisions cannot occur.

Implementers MUST ensure that after validation only attributes the issuer is trusted to issue are used in authorization decisions, and other attributes, which may be present, must be ignored. Because the AA controls extension is optional to implement, verifiers must be given that information by other means, such as configuration, which matters when a verifier trusts more than one issuer. Implementers SHOULD also be very careful in mapping the authenticated identity to the certificate holder, especially when the authenticated identity does not come from a public key certificate, since the link between identity and certificate may not be as strong.
sections.plainLanguage: The risks here are the usual ones for certificate systems: a stolen signing key lets an attacker mint permissions, an old certificate may still look valid when it should not, and two authorities with the same name can confuse the check that binds a certificate to its holder. The document lists the measures that address each of them.
